Your first two weeks with me

Pick where you are. This is what I would do with you in the first two weeks.

  1. Week 1List what a buyer will ask for in due diligence, and where each answer lives today: a system, a spreadsheet or your head.
  2. Week 2The three things most likely to cut the price, named with owners and dates, and the first one already being fixed.

You get: you learn what costs you money in the sale years before a buyer tells you.

  1. Week 1Map the decisions and knowledge only you hold: pricing, key customers, suppliers, the jobs nobody else can quote.
  2. Week 2The first of them handed to a person or a simple system, with you checking the work instead of doing it.

You get: the business keeps its pace in the weeks you are not there.

  1. Week 1Trace where the monthly numbers really come from, and which spreadsheets disagree with each other.
  2. Week 2A monthly close and a short scorecard running from one source, ready to show a buyer as they are.

You get: numbers a buyer can trust without sending in a team to rebuild them.

  1. Week 1Who could run what: sales, operations, finance. Where the gaps are and what each role would own.
  2. Week 2Roles agreed, a weekly meeting with a scorecard, and the first decisions made without you in the room.

You get: a team a buyer can see and wants to keep, not a business that leaves with its founder.

Hands on, now

I write and ship the software myself. Two things I am building alongside, for society and the state:

Ruminator

Reads Russia's regional and local press every day, from state television to residents' channels, and shows what each kind of outlet reports and how it frames it. Every claim is checked word for word against the source. For analysts, journalists and diplomats.

LedgerGov.UK

An open P&L of the UK state: where public money comes from, where it goes and what every political promise would cost, each number linked to its official source.

My code is public at github.com/xternal.

Who I am

Pavel Guzhikov, London. Twenty years of building companies, as founder and as the person who makes them run. I've built companies at every stage: from zero, through scaling and profit, to a sale. I founded and sold two companies myself, so I know what a buyer looks for and what makes them take money off the price. I was on the founding team at Uzum, Uzbekistan's first unicorn: lending, payments, cards and a marketplace for millions of users. Along the way I've rebuilt a company's processes from zero in a new country and taken a business from loss to profit in six months. I'm hands-on in the technology, the product and the business.

What stays yours

The company, the decisions and the timing. I am not a broker and I don't sell your company: I make it worth more, whoever you sell to and whenever you choose. Your team needs to know only that we are making the business run better, which is true. You get a short weekly note: what moved, what is stuck, what needs your decision.

Questions

When should I start?
Two or three years before a sale is best: long enough for the changes to show in the accounts a buyer reads. Later still helps, but a buyer sees the last two or three years.
Do you help with the sale itself?
No. Your corporate finance adviser runs the sale. I make the business worth more and easier to buy, and I'm happy to work alongside them.
Which companies?
Owner-run British businesses from about 20 to a few hundred people: manufacturers, distributors, contractors, producers, service firms.
Interim manager, adviser or consultant?
A hands-on operator. I run the work with your team and write the software where it helps. No decks: processes that run differently the following week.
Is it confidential?
Yes. Nobody outside needs to know you are thinking about a sale.

What would a buyer see today? 30 minutes.
